cls: Vaccine - poliomyelitis (inactivated, IPV; or oral live-attenuated, OPV)
pharm: Immunising agent that induces neutralising antibodies against poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3 to prevent paralytic poliomyelitis
quick: IPV 0.5 mL IM/SC per dose; primary series and boosters per schedule (adults at risk: 3-dose series)
Not applicable - injection (IPV); OPV drops given orally irrespective of feeds
IPV may be given if indicated; avoid routine vaccination unless at risk
IPV and OPV are compatible with breastfeeding
Observe for immediate hypersensitivity; document the dose in the immunisation record
summary: Polio vaccine prevents poliomyelitis by inducing protective neutralising antibodies against poliovirus serotypes 1, 2 and 3. Two forms are used: inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV, e.g. IPOL), a killed-virus injectable vaccine given subcutaneously or intramuscularly in a 0.5 mL dose, and oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV), a live-attenuated vaccine given as oral drops, used in many national immunisation programmes (now mainly bivalent types 1 and 3). The primary childhood series is given at the schedule's recommended ages with later boosters; previously unvaccinated adults at increased risk (travel to endemic areas, laboratory or healthcare exposure) receive a three-dose IPV series. IPV is the preferred vaccine for immunocompromised individuals and their household contacts because it carries no risk of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP), a very rare complication of the live OPV. Polio vaccines are biologics regulated under vaccine (not the openFDA drug/label) pathways; the details here follow the manufacturer package insert, WHO and national immunisation guidance.
indications: Active immunisation against poliomyelitis (types 1, 2 and 3) in infants, children and at-risk adults
Routine childhood immunisation per the national schedule
Pre-exposure protection for adults at increased risk (travellers to endemic/epidemic areas, laboratory and healthcare workers)

dosage.d: 0.5 mL per dose; primary doses (commonly at 2, 4 and 6-18 months) with a booster (commonly at 4-6 years)
Bivalent OPV (types 1 and 3) drops orally per the programme schedule (e.g. birth dose plus primary doses)
dosage.n: Per national programme; IPV is co-administered in many schedules

dosage.d: Three 0.5 mL doses: two doses 1-2 months apart and a third 6-12 months after the second
dosage.n: A single booster for previously vaccinated adults at ongoing risk

admin: Give IPV as a 0.5 mL subcutaneous or intramuscular injection; give OPV as oral drops
Administer per the national/WHO immunisation schedule and record the dose, batch and date in the immunisation record
May be given with other routine vaccines at separate sites
Have facilities to manage an immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reaction available; observe after vaccination
Use IPV (not live OPV) for immunocompromised people and their close/household contacts
moa: Polio vaccines stimulate the immune system to produce neutralising antibodies against the three poliovirus serotypes. Inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) contains killed virus that induces humoral (serum) antibody, providing individual protection against paralytic disease. Oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) contains live-attenuated virus that replicates in the gut, inducing both serum and intestinal (mucosal) immunity, which limits transmission - an advantage in outbreak control, but at the cost of a very rare risk of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis and vaccine-derived poliovirus.

absolute: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or to a vaccine component (IPV may contain trace neomycin, streptomycin, polymyxin B)
For OPV: known immunodeficiency in the recipient or a household contact (use IPV instead)
relative: Moderate or severe acute illness (defer until recovered); minor illness is not a contraindication
Pregnancy (defer routine vaccination unless at increased risk)
monitor: Observe for immediate hypersensitivity after administration
Document the dose in the immunisation record
For OPV programmes, monitor for vaccine-associated paralysis (very rare)

preg: Although there is no convincing evidence of harm, routine polio vaccination is usually deferred in pregnancy. If a pregnant woman is at increased risk of exposure, IPV (the inactivated vaccine) may be given.
lact: Polio vaccines (IPV and OPV) are compatible with breastfeeding; breastfeeding does not interfere with the immune response.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

moderate: Immunosuppressants/high-dose corticosteroids and immunodeficiency - may blunt the immune response; live OPV is contraindicated in immunosuppression
minor: May be co-administered with other routine vaccines at separate injection sites
interactions.food: Not applicable for IPV; OPV is given irrespective of feeding

common: Irritability, drowsiness, reduced appetite in infants
serious: Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) - very rare, with live OPV only
rare: Vaccine-derived poliovirus emergence in under-immunised populations (OPV, programmatic concern)
emergency: Acute flaccid paralysis after OPV (very rare - seek urgent assessment)

monitoring: Observation for immediate allergic reactions after administration
Completion of the schedule and recording of doses
Surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis in OPV programmes
counsel: This vaccine protects against polio, a virus that can cause paralysis; the full course and boosters are needed for lasting protection
Mild soreness at the injection site, low fever or irritability for a day or two is common and settles
Tell the clinic if the child is immunocompromised or lives with someone who is, so the injected (inactivated) vaccine is used
Seek urgent help for any severe allergic reaction (difficulty breathing, swelling, collapse) shortly after vaccination
Keep the immunisation record up to date
pk: Protective antibody develops over about 1-2 weeks after the priming doses
Robust antibody titres after completion of the primary series
Not applicable - vaccine induces lasting immune memory rather than measurable drug levels
Long-lasting, generally lifelong immunity after a complete series; boosters reinforce protection
Store refrigerated at 2-8 C; do not freeze IPV; protect from light and follow cold-chain requirements
pearls: Two forms: inactivated IPV (injection, serum immunity, no VAPP risk) and live OPV (oral, mucosal immunity, used in programmes)
Use IPV - not live OPV - for immunocompromised people and their household contacts
VAPP and vaccine-derived poliovirus are very rare risks of OPV only; IPV carries no such risk
Regulated as a biologic/vaccine (not via openFDA drug/label); details follow manufacturer insert, WHO and national schedules
Complete the primary series plus boosters; IPV can be given to at-risk pregnant women
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed, give it at the next opportunity and continue from where the schedule left off - the series does not need to be restarted. Keep the immunisation record updated.
overdose: Overdose is not a meaningful concern with vaccines; inadvertent extra doses are not expected to cause harm beyond the usual local/systemic reactions. Manage any reaction supportively.
